figures.title: One query's row: score, softmax, weighted sum
figures.caption: A query scores three keys with dot products 2, 1 and 0. Softmax turns those scores into shares 0.665, 0.245 and 0.090, and the shares weight the values into the output (0.755, 0.335). The row is a differentiable lookup: the query is the lookup key, the keys are the indices, the values are the contents.
figures.alt: A four-column table. The columns are: project x into q, k and v; score the query against each key; softmax the row; and sum the weighted values. Three value rows show v1 equals (1, 0) scoring 2 and taking share 0.665, v2 equals (0, 1) scoring 1 and taking 0.245, and v3 equals (1, 1) scoring 0 and taking 0.090. The output row shows the weighted sum (0.755, 0.335).

data.note: exp(2), exp(1), exp(0) = 7.389, 2.718, 1.000, sum 11.107; shares 0.665, 0.245, 0.090. The output is the share-weighted sum of the values. Scaling by 1/sqrt(d_k) is the next figure.

steps.label: Each token's x is projected into q, k and v.
The query scores every key with a dot product.
Softmax turns the row of scores into shares.
The shares weight the values and sum to the output.

figures.title: Why divide by sqrt(d_k)
figures.caption: Score standard deviation against d_k under the paper's unit-variance assumption: the raw curve is sqrt(d_k), and the horizontal line is the scaled result, standard deviation 1. At d_k = 64 the raw standard deviation is 8, so a two-sigma gap between the top two scores gives an exponential ratio of about 8.9 million; dividing by sqrt(d_k) shrinks the gap by 8. The curve is computed from sqrt(d_k), not measured.
figures.alt: A log-log plot. The rising line is score standard deviation equal to square root of d_k, passing through d_k equals 1 with standard deviation 1, d_k equals 16 with 4, d_k equals 64 with 8, and d_k equals 4096 with 64. A horizontal line at standard deviation 1 is labelled after dividing by square root of d_k. A point at d_k equals 64, standard deviation 8 is labelled.

data.note: Under the assumption each product q_a k_a has variance 1, and the sum of d_k products has variance d_k, so the raw score standard deviation is sqrt(d_k). A gap of two standard deviations gives e^16 ≈ 8.9 million; at a = 0.999 the softmax gradient is 0.000999, against 0.223 in the unsaturated example. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores standard deviation 1.
